stem: Which of the following is most correct:

options.html: Warfarin levels are monitored using aPTT
Unfractionated heparin levels are monitored using aPTT
Low molecular weight heparin levels are monitored using aPTT
Rivaroxaban levels are monitored using aPTT
More than one of the above is correct

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Correct! Unfractionated heparin affects both factors IIa and Xa, but has a predominant effect on the intrinsic pathway, and thus prolongs the aPTT. The therapeutic range is 60-80 seconds. Option A is false - recall that warfarin interferes with the vitamin K dependent coagulation factors (II, VII, IX, X, as well as protein C &S). INR evaluates factors VII, X, V, and II (extrinsic and common pathway), while aPTT evaluates factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II and fibrinogen (intrinsic and common pathway). Although warfarin may also affect the aPTT, INR is used to monitor warfarin effects rather than measuring both. Option C is false - not only does LMWH not usually require monitoring, but also the shorter fragments present in LMWH have a much greater effect on Xa than on IIa, and therefore do not significantly affect the aPTT. This also means that protamine sulphate is only a partial antidote to LWMH. If it is necessary to monitor LWMH, heparin activation can be measured. Option D is false - Rivaroxaban only affects Xa, and therefore does not significantly affect the aPTT.

stem: Which of the following does not cause HIT:
answer:
The correct answer is C.

A. No, unfractionated heparin is the worst culprit for HIT (that’s why it’s called “heparin induced thrombocytopenia), as it is caused by antibodies to heparin which also have an affinity for platelets. HIT usually occurs 5-14 days after the initiation of heparin, and when this happens you need to substitute another anticoagulant! B. No, although LMWH is a much better choice than unfractionated heparin in terms of risk for HIT, it can still cause the same antibody response. C. Correct! Fondiparinux has no antigenic cross-reactivity with heparin. It can also be used to treat HIT.

stem: You are evaluating a hospital inpatient, and the Well’s criteria for DVT indicates that it’s unlikely. Your next best step in working up the patient is:

options.html: Compression ultrasound, because if negative it rules out DVT
Compression ultrasound, because it is likely to be positive
D-dimer, because if positive, it indicates that DVT is present
D-dimer, because if negative it rules out DVT
No investigations related to DVT are warranted in this situation

answer:
The correct answer is D.

A. No – while compression u/s is more than 90% sensitive for proximal DVT, one negative result is not sufficient to exclude DVT. B. No – compression ultrasound is generally reserved for patients in whom the pre-test probability of DVT is high, and this question indicated a diagnosis of DVT would be unlikely. Even if it were done in this patient, since the clinical suspicion was that DVT is unlikely, by definition we would not expect it to be positive. If the patient had a positive ddimer (which is quite common in hospital inpatients), a U/S would then be indicated. C. No – the d-dimer test we commonly use is very sensitive but not specific for clot formation, and can therefore rule out but not rule in DVT. Most inpatients are unlikely to have a negative test, even if they do not have DVT. D. Yes! A negative d-dimer excludes the diagnosis of DVT without the requirement for any more tests, because of its high sensitivity. In a hospital inpatient it is unlikely to be negative, but if it is, you can safely exclude DVT. E. Even though in this case your clinical suspicion is that DVT is unlikely, DVT is a diagnosis that you don’t want to miss, so you should at least order a d-dimer, which, if negative, will rule out the diagnosis.

stem: Which of the following is not characteristic of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML):

options.html: Lack of mature cells (ie mainly blasts) in the peripheral blood/bone marrow
Insidious presentation and non-specific symptoms that may include fatigue, weakness, weight loss, night sweats, LUQ pain

answer:
The correct answer is B.

A. No – splenomegaly is the most common physical finding in CML, and may be responsible for some of the other non-specific symptoms such as LUQ pain/fullness, early satiety B. Yes – CML is an insidious process. Although a left shift may be present, a large proportion of blasts would be suggestive of an acute leukemia. Note that CML may eventually lead to a blast crisis, which is essentially a conversion to either AML (2/3) or ALL (1/3). C. No – a significant proportion of patients are actually asymptomatic at diagnosis, but if there are symptoms they are general non-specific and develop slowly over time. D. No – the Philadelphia chromosome is the underlying, acquired, cytogenetic defect in CML. The t(9;22) translocation creates a melds the genes BCR (chr. 22) and ABL (chromosome 9), creating an oncogene (due to loss of appropriate regulation) that produces a tyrosine kinase enzyme involved in cell growth regulation. E. No – CML will increase WBC, and a differential would demonstrate disproportionate increase in granulocytes, since they are the WBCs in the myeloid lineage.

options.html: Whether neoplasm is of myeloid or lymphoid origin

answer:
The correct answer is E.

Note that this is the only answer that is not a property of an individual cell – to characterize architecture, the grouping of cells within the tissue must be intact, which is not possible in flow cytometry. stem: Which of the following situations would be best suited to an excisional lymph node biopsy:

options.html: A patient who would only want the most minimally invasive procedure to diagnose
Need cytogenetics, flow analysis and suspect minimal disease

answer:
The correct answer is E.

Excisional biopsy provides plenty of tissue for analyses such as flow cytometry and cytogenetics, and because it removes the entire node, we are able to pick up even minimal disease, that might be missed if we just sampled the node in a core or FNA biopsy. It also allows us to describe the architecture of the tissue, unlike FNAB. However, in a patient who is very sick (not a candidate for surgery) (c), or when there is no OR available (b), it is not the best choice. For patients who will only accept the most minimally invasive proedure needed to diagnose a mass, a FNAB provides a quick alternative method that does not require an OR(a). If the tumour is in certain critical locations (d), it may not be possible to remove it, and thus an excisional biopsy would not be appropriate.

stem: Which of the following characteristics is most suggestive of a malignant lymph node enlargement:
answer:
The correct answer is E.

A. No – the larger the node, the more concerning (in general). For most lymph nodes, size >2.5cm is something you should pay attention to. If the node is in the popliteal fossa, if it is epitrochlear, or if it’s infraclavicular, begin to worry much earlier – they should not be larger than 0.5cm! B. stem: Carcinogenesis occurs in a predictable sequence. Which of the following represents the typical progression from a normal cell to a metastatic lesion.

options.html: normal--> carcinoma in situ --> moderate dysplasia--> severe dysplasia--> invasive carcinoma --> regional metastasis--> distant metastasis
normal--> mild dysplasia--> moderate dysplasia--> severe dysplasia--> carcinoma in situ--> invasive carcinoma--> regional metastasis--> distant metastasis
normal--> angiogenesis--> mild dysplasia--> moderate dysplasia--> severe dysplasia--> invasive carcinoma --> distant metastasis --> regional metastasis
normal-->angiogenesis--> dysplasia--> metaplasia--> aplasia--> carcinoma in situ--> invasive carcinoma--> regional metastasis--> distant metastasis
normal--> dysplasia --> angiogenesis --> aplasia --> metaplasia --> carcinoma in situ--> invasive carcinoma--> regional metastasis--> distant metastasis

answer:
The correct answer is B.

This represents the typical progression from a normal cell to a cancerous lesion. Dysplasia refers to a cell losing its normal cellular shape, size or orientation. Specifically, dysplasia refers to four microscopic changes: 1) hyperchromatism (excessive pigmentation) 2) Poikilocytosis (abnormal shaped cells) 3) Anisocytosis (cells of unequal size) 4) Presence of mitotic figures (increased # cells undergoing mitosis at any given time). Progression from carcinoma in situ to invasive carcinoma requires the neoplastic lesion to breach the basement membrane. Once this has been achieved, the malignant lesion is free to metastasize to regional lymph nodes and structures before metastasizing to distant sites. It is for this reason that the presence of distant metastasis yields the worst prognosis because it is assumed to already have infiltrated regional lymph nodes and surrounding anatomy by the time the metastasis is evident

stem: Upon conducting a physical exam of the previous patient (in Q80), he has 3 enlarged lymph nodes in the left cervical region, and one enlarged left infraclavicular node as well. You astutely suspect Hodgkin’s lymphoma. Based on the modified Ann Arbour staging system, what is this patient’s stage:
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Stage I is a single lymph node region involved (or single extralymphatic site, which would require an ‘E’ at the end). Stage II involves two or more lymph node regions on the same side of the diaphragm. Stage III Involves 2+ lymph nodes regions on both sides of the diaphragm, +/- the spleen. Stage IV is diffuse involvement of one or more extralymphatic organs. This patient has involvement of the cervical and infraclavicular regions (note that if the regions involved are not contiguous, we would not be dealing with a Hodgkin’s lymphoma), which makes 2 regions, and both are above the diaphragm, so he has stage II disease. The “A” or “B” suffix indicates the absence (A) or presence (B) of B-symptoms (unexplained recurrent fever, unexplained weight loss >10% body weight in last 6 months, drenching night sweats). This patient’s night sweats sound “drenching”, so we call him a stage IIB.
